newsitem.title: USA: Selection of Oklahoma trial jury nearly complete.
newsitem.headline: Selection of Oklahoma trial jury nearly complete.

text.p: Selection of 12 jurors to hear the murder and conspiracy case against accused Oklahoma City bomber Timothy McVeigh neared completion on Tuesday as defence and prosecution lawyers began striking potential jurors from the final pool of candidates.

Lawyers for each side spent the morning exercising 22 of their 23 so-called peremptory challenges, which allow them to strike potential jurors without giving a specific reason. The process was expected to be complete by mid-afternoon.

The identities of the potential jurors have been kept a closely guarded secret, with each candidate referred to by an elaborate numbering system. The calling out of jurors in the packed federal courtroom by numbers such as B-3 and A-8 prompted chief prosecutor Joseph Hartzler to remark lightheartedly, "Ever play Bingo, your honour?"
His quip evoked a stern response from U.S. District Court Judge Richard Matsch, who said, "It's a lot more serious than a Bingo game."

Potential jurors have been identifed by numbers since the interview process began on March 31. But the judge shuffled their numbers overnight, making it impossible to determine even the most basic facts, such as gender, about them.

The 12 jurors and six alternates will not be sequestered during the trial of McVeigh, who is accused of blowing up the Alfred P. Murrah federal building in Oklahoma City on April 19, 1995, killing 168 people including 19 children, many of whom were at a day care centre in the building.
McVeigh, a Gulf War Army veteran, has pleaded not guilty in the worst-ever attack on civilians on U.S. soil. He faces the death penalty if convicted.

The tall, pale defendant, wearing a dark blue shirt, khaki slacks and a crewcut, appeared to be actively participating in his defence. He busily took notes and jotted messages on slips of paper for his attorneys.

During a break, members of some of the victim's families chatted quietly outside the courthouse with one another. They included Roy Sells, whose wife Lee died in the blast, and Marsha Kight, who lost her daughter, Frankie Merrell.

Matsch denied a request by McVeigh's lawyers to delay the trial because of heavy publicity on the second anniversary of the tragedy. Chief defence attorney Stephen Jones argued a delay was necessary due to "massive media portrayals of the second anniversary of the Oklahoma City bombing."

While observances of the anniversary last Saturday in Denver and around the nation were appropriate, Jones said, they took place during "a sensitive period" when potenial jurors were being interviewed. Observances in Denver included ringing of church bells 168 times, once for each of the dead.
Opening arguments were expected to begin on Thursday, leaving Wednesday as a day off for jurors to get their personal affairs in order. Wednesday is also McVeigh's 29th birthday.
